Tensor order and integral kernel bounds

Reconstructed and self-checked by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, October 2026. Earlier edition: GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort. Original exposition: CC0. Supplied foundations retain their stated licences.

An integral kernel can describe evaluation on a graph, differentiation of an input, or averaging over a region. Its absolute row and column integrals control all its bounds. For distributional kernels, a different issue is the number of test derivatives needed to bound a pairing. Tensor products can attain the sum of two orders, but sufficiently separated frequencies can reduce that exact order to their maximum.

We pair distributions complex linearly, so . The test topology and local finite-order estimates are proved in U008, the initial test-space construction and Proposition 1.2. The complete tensor construction on arbitrary Euclidean open sets is U021, B0–B2, especially (B5)–(B6). That proof includes density of sums of product tests, tensor uniqueness, exact product supports and three-factor associativity. These exact supplied results suffice here.

The scalar foundation, §§12, 13.1–13.5 and 13.7–13.10, proves compactness, calculus, exponential/trigonometric series and smooth cutoffs. The finite algebra foundation, §§10.1–10.6, proves the inner-product and matrix identities. The integration foundation, §§15.0–15.3 and 16, proves completed Lebesgue integration, Tonelli, Fubini, Hölder and measurable sections. All further estimates and sharpness arguments are proved below.

Evaluation and differentiation determine a kernel

For an operator , a kernel means a distribution on satisfying There is at most one such distribution: subtract two and apply the product-test density proved in U021 B2. In the following cases we construct it explicitly.

Theorem 1.1 (continuous graph evaluation). For every continuous real , let . Then This is an order-zero positive graph measure, with exact support . Its operator is , which is weakly continuous from tests to distributions.

Proof. The function is Borel and bounded. For a test supported in a compact rectangle , absolute Fubini and the fundamental theorem give The first integrand vanishes outside , so is absolutely integrable. The second pairing is bounded by . Thus it has order at most zero. It is integration against the pushforward of by the continuous map ; the same estimate gives local finiteness.

The graph is closed: if , continuity forces . Off it, the pairing vanishes on a sufficiently small neighborhood. At , choose a nonnegative smooth test supported in any prescribed neighborhood and positive on a smaller rectangle around that point. Continuity of places in that smaller rectangle for all in a nonempty interval about . Its pairing is strictly positive. The support is therefore exactly the graph and the measure is nonzero, so its exact order is zero.

On product tests the formula is , proving the operator identity and uniqueness. The output is continuous. For every fixed , This bound gives continuity for the test topology and hence weak continuity into distributions. The argument has made no assumption on derivatives, injectivity or properness of .

Row and column masses control every exponent

Theorem 2.1 (Schur bounds, with every endpoint). Let and be open. Suppose the measurable complex kernel satisfies where . For every , the integral converges absolutely for almost every , defines a measurable output class, and obeys These bounds are valid on almost-everywhere equivalence classes and are sharp as universal bounds. If either or is zero, the kernel and every operator are zero almost everywhere.

Proof: measurable representatives. Open Euclidean sets with Lebesgue measure are sigma-finite. We first justify the choice of Borel representatives. The integration foundation, §15.0, proves that each Lebesgue measurable set differs from a Borel set inside a Borel null set. Approximate a nonnegative measurable function by the increasing finite simple functions of §16.1. Replace every level set in this countable family by its Borel version. The new simple functions agree with the old ones off one Borel null union; their pointwise limit there, extended by zero on that union, is a Borel representative. Split real and imaginary parts into positive and negative parts to treat finite complex functions. This applies on the product space as well as each factor.

Changing a representative on a null set preserves its section integrals outside a null set, by Tonelli and completion. For the input assertion directly, if off a null set , then Indeed is product null by a countable finite-measure exhaustion of . Tonelli gives zero integral on almost every row. The same argument applies to two versions of which agree almost everywhere. We may take finite representatives throughout.

Integrals of nonnegative Borel functions over one variable are measurable by Tonelli. Real and imaginary parts, split into positive and negative parts, consequently give a measurable complex integral wherever it is absolutely finite. Set the output to zero on the exceptional null set.

Proof: norm estimates. If , Tonelli on gives integral zero for ; exhaustion gives almost everywhere. If , interchange the two variables in this reasoning. A zero kernel gives zero on almost every row for every input, as above.

For , Tonelli gives Thus the inner integral is finite almost everywhere and yields the first bound. For , put Its integral is at most , so it is finite almost everywhere. Hölder in the ordinary measure, applied to and , gives on such rows Zero rows are interpreted directly as zero; all remaining rows have finite weight. Raising to and integrating proves This simultaneously proves absolute existence. At infinity choose a representative bounded by ; the absolute row integral is at most . Representative independence transfers the conclusion to the entire class. Linearity follows on the intersection of the full-measure sets where the finite collection of relevant integrals converges.

These are universal estimates; a particular complex kernel can have a smaller interior norm.

A nonzero factor reveals its own order

For an integer , a distribution has order at most if every compact test support has a constant such that The same must work for all supports; only the constants vary. The exact order is the least such nonnegative integer, when one exists. We assign zero distribution order zero.

Theorem 3.1 (upper bound and converse). For distributions on arbitrary Euclidean open sets , orders at most imply tensor order at most . If both factors are nonzero and their tensor has order at most , each factor has order at most .

Proof. Every compact subset of lies in the product of its compact projections. U021 (B6), with the two given order estimates, gives Each derivative has total order at most . This proves the upper bound on every compact support.

For the converse, choose a fixed test with , by rescaling a nonzero pairing. On any compact , apply the tensor order bound to . Each derivative of total order at most is a product of a derivative of through and a fixed derivative of . Hence The same argument with a normalized test of gives the estimate for . It includes . If one factor is zero, its tensor is zero regardless of the order of the other factor, so the converse hypothesis is necessary.

Separated frequencies attain the maximum order

We will use the elementary fact that for each integer and real . The quotient of consecutive terms is , which tends to by the finite binomial formula. Choose strictly between these numbers and one. Beyond a fixed index the terms are bounded by a fixed multiple of ; the finite geometric-sum formula bounds that tail. This proves the fact without a further convergence criterion.

Theorem 5.1 (the maximum can be the exact order). For every integer , there are two distributions on , each of exact order , whose tensor product also has exact order .

Proof: defining the factors. Let and define the two series by pairing their even and odd modes with tests: For a test supported in an interval of length , integration by parts times has no boundary terms and yields After multiplying by , the summable bound is a constant times . The series therefore defines a linear functional with an order- estimate on every compact test support. It is a distribution by the supplied test topology; tails converge in that same seminorm estimate.

Proof: detecting the factor orders. Choose a nonnegative smooth supported compactly in and positive on . The supplied cutoff construction gives such a function. Splitting its integral into unit intervals gives for every integer The final integral follows from the scalar exponential primitive and . There are only finitely many contributing translated pieces.

For of the chosen parity, put Leibniz's rule bounds all derivatives through independently of , since every resulting power of has exponent at most zero. The support is fixed. The already absolutely convergent pairing series and the integer-frequency identity give exactly All other frequencies have zero pairing. Both parities contain arbitrarily large , so neither factor has order at most .

Proof: the tensor estimate. Form the double mode series with even and odd . For a two-variable test supported in a rectangle of area , integrate by parts times in the variable with the larger frequency: The indices cannot coincide. Thus the coefficient majorant is Dropping the parity restriction while retaining distinct indices bounds this by The equality uses . The last convergence follows from for , proved by induction using , and the elementary summability just proved for the dominating . This supplies a finite order- bound for the double series.

On a product test, absolute convergence of each one-variable series factors the double sum into the two pairings. U021 B2 therefore identifies the resulting distribution with on all tests. Each factor is nonzero and has exact order ; Theorem 3.1 excludes a smaller tensor order. This proves the claim, also for .
